title: Undoing Changes & Recovery
summary: Every stage of git — working tree, staging, history, pushed history — has its own undo tool, and using the wrong one either fails silently or destroys work. Learn to match the tool to the stage, plus the reflog safety net underneath all of it.

slides.markdown:
Mistakes happen at every stage of git's workflow — an edit you regret before staging it, a file staged by accident, a commit that shouldn't exist, a push that needs to disappear from a shared branch. Each stage has a **different correct undo tool**, and git's biggest undo trap is using the wrong one: `reset` where you needed `revert`, or `checkout` where you needed `restore`.

The organizing idea for this whole topic: figure out which of git's three trees — working directory, staging area, commit history — holds the change you want gone, then reach for the tool built for exactly that stage. Get that match wrong and you either do nothing, or you silently discard work with no undo.

slides.sectionTitle: Matching the tool to the stage
slides.markdown:
Every undo question reduces to one first step: **where does the unwanted change currently live?**

- **Working directory only** (edited, not staged) → `git restore <file>` throws away the edit.
- **Staged** (added, not committed) → `git restore --staged <file>` unstages it, keeping the edit in the working directory.
- **Committed, not pushed** → `git reset` can remove the commit from your branch entirely, keeping or discarding its changes depending on mode.
- **Committed and pushed, others may have it** → `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes the old one, without erasing history anyone already has.

The further right you go on this list, the more "undo" starts meaning "add a new commit that cancels the old one" rather than "make it as if it never happened" — because once something is shared, erasing it isn't safe or even possible for everyone who already has it.

slides.subTitle: For unstaged and staged changes
slides.markdown:
| | Unstages a file | Discards working-directory edits | Modern or legacy |
|---|---|---|
| `git restore --staged <file>` | Yes | No | Modern (git 2.23+) |
| `git restore <file>` | N/A | Yes | Modern |
| `git checkout -- <file>` | No | Yes | Legacy, same effect as `restore` |
| `git reset <file>` | Yes | No | Legacy, same effect as `restore --staged` |

`restore` and `switch` were split out of the old, overloaded `checkout` specifically because `checkout` did unrelated things — switch branches, restore files, detach HEAD — under one command, and people confused them under pressure, especially `checkout <commit> -- <file>` silently doing something different from `checkout <branch>`. The legacy forms still work everywhere and appear constantly in older docs, but `restore`/`switch` are what to write and teach today.

slides.subTitle: What moves — HEAD, index, working tree
slides.markdown:
`git reset <commit>` moves your branch pointer to a different commit, but the three modes differ in how much else they touch:

- **`--soft`** — moves HEAD only. Your staged changes and working directory are untouched, so the "undone" commits' changes now sit staged, ready to be recommitted differently.
- **`--mixed`** (the default) — moves HEAD and resets the staging area to match. Changes move from staged back to just present in the working directory.
- **`--hard`** — moves HEAD, resets staging, **and overwrites the working directory** to match. Any uncommitted edits and the undone commits' changes are gone from disk, not just unstaged.

The practical read: `--soft` is for "I want to redo how I committed this, keep everything staged." `--mixed` is for "unstage everything, let me re-add selectively." `--hard` is for "I genuinely want this gone from disk," and it's the only one of the three that can destroy uncommitted work with no prompt.

slides.sectionTitle: `git revert` — undoing via a new commit
slides.markdown:
`git revert <commit>` doesn't remove anything from history — it creates a **new commit** whose diff is the exact inverse of the target commit's changes. History grows by one commit; nothing before it is altered or renamed.

```bash
git revert a1b2c3d
# creates a new commit: "Revert 'Add rate limiter middleware'"
```

This is what makes revert safe on a shared branch: because it's purely additive, everyone who already has the original commit is unaffected by it — they just pull the new revert commit on top, same as any other commit. There's no rewritten hash, no force-push required, no risk of clobbering someone else's work. If the original commit was itself a merge commit, `revert -m` is needed to specify which parent's changes to treat as the "mainline" being reverted from.

slides.subTitle: Local cleanup vs public-history-safe undo
slides.markdown:
| | `git reset` | `git revert` |
|---|---|---|
| Rewrites history | Yes — moves the branch pointer, can drop commits | No — adds a new commit |
| Safe if others already have the commit | No | Yes |
| Result | Branch looks as if the commit never happened | Branch shows both the original commit and its undo |
| Typical use | Cleaning up your own local, unpushed commits | Undoing something already merged to a shared branch |

The decision is really the same golden rule from [Rebase vs Merge](rebase-vs-merge) applied to undoing instead of rewriting: reset only what's still purely yours, revert anything already shared. Reverting a commit only you have is harmless but usually unnecessary — reset is simpler there. Resetting a commit others already have recreates the exact clobbering problem a shared force-push does.

`git stash` saves your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) onto a hidden stack and restores a clean working directory — useful when you need to switch branches urgently without committing half-finished work.

```bash
git stash              # save changes, clean working directory
git stash pop          # restore the most recent stash, remove it from the stack
git stash apply        # restore the most recent stash, keep it on the stack
git stash list          # see everything currently stashed
git stash drop          # discard a stash entry without applying it
```

`pop` and `apply` differ in exactly one thing: whether the stash entry is removed after restoring. Prefer `apply` when you're not fully sure the restore will go conflict-free — if it does conflict, the stash stays safely on the stack rather than being consumed on a failed attempt. Stashes are stored as real (if unusual) git commits internally, which is why they survive things like a `reset --hard` on your working tree.

slides.subTitle: Git's safety net for "unreachable" commits
slides.markdown:
Deleting a branch or running `reset --hard` doesn't actually destroy the commit objects immediately — it just moves pointers so those commits are no longer *reachable* from any branch or tag. Git still keeps them around for a grace period (default 90 days for reachable-then-orphaned commits, 30 for genuinely dangling ones) before garbage collection ever removes them.

The **reflog** (`git reflog`) is your local, per-repository log of everywhere HEAD has pointed — every commit, checkout, reset, and rebase step, in order, each with a timestamp:

```
e4f5g6h HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
a1b2c3d HEAD@{1}: commit: Add rate limiter middleware
```

That `HEAD@{1}` entry is a real, working reference to a commit that a branch may no longer point to — which is exactly what makes "unreachable" commits recoverable, as long as the reflog entry still exists and gc hasn't run. The reflog is local-only; it isn't pushed and doesn't exist on the remote or for anyone else's clone.

slides.sectionTitle: Recovering a deleted branch or lost commit
slides.markdown:
```bash
# find the commit — look for its message or hash in the reflog
git reflog
# e4f5g6h HEAD@{2}: commit: Add rate limiter middleware

# recreate the branch pointing at it
git branch recovered-feature e4f5g6h

# or, if you're trying to undo a reset you just did on the current branch
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
```

This works because the commit object itself was never deleted — only the pointer that made it reachable was moved or removed. `git branch <name> <hash>` (or `<name> HEAD@{n}`) simply creates a new pointer at that exact commit, and everything reachable from it — the whole commit chain behind it — comes back intact.

If you don't remember the exact hash, `git fsck --unreachable` lists every commit object git still has that isn't reachable from any branch or tag, which is a broader (slower) search than scanning the reflog by eye.

`git reset --hard` is the one undo command with no safety net for uncommitted changes: it overwrites the working directory to match the target commit, discarding any edits that were never committed — staged or not — with no prompt and no reflog entry, because the reflog only tracks commits, not uncommitted edits.

This is different from resetting away *committed* work, which the reflog can recover. An uncommitted edit that `reset --hard` wipes out was never a commit object at all, so there's nothing for the reflog to point back to. The only real protections are `git stash` beforehand (if you might want the edits back) or simply committing early and often — a bad commit is recoverable; a discarded uncommitted edit generally isn't.

The habit worth building: before running any `--hard` reset, run `git status` and confirm there's nothing in the working directory you'd regret losing.

Everything in this topic operates on git's object model at a fairly practical level — commits, branches, the reflog as a list of where HEAD has been. The next topic, **Advanced Git Internals**, goes one level deeper: the actual object types (blob, tree, commit, tag) that all of this is built from, how git stores and compresses them, and the power tools — `bisect`, `cherry-pick` — that a genuinely fluent user reaches for beyond day-to-day undo operations.
